title: Imperial Russia, revolution and the Soviet state (1855–1924)
summary: Reform and reaction under Alexander II, Alexander III and Nicholas II, the revolutions of 1905 and 1917, and how the Bolsheviks won the civil war and built the Soviet state.

keyterms.definition: Alexander II's 1861 edict freeing about 23 million privately owned serfs, who then paid redemption payments for land.
Elected local councils created in 1864 to run schools, roads and health care, dominated by the gentry.
Policy, especially under Alexander III, of imposing Russian language, religion and culture on national minorities.
Finance minister (1892–1903) who drove rapid industrialisation through foreign loans, tariffs and railways such as the Trans-Siberian.
Nicholas II's 1905 promise of civil liberties and an elected Duma, which split the opposition.
Prime minister (1906–11) who combined harsh repression with land reforms creating independent peasant farmers.
Uneasy sharing of authority in 1917 between the Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet.
Lenin's April 1917 programme: no support for the Provisional Government, 'all power to the Soviets', peace and land.
Bolshevik civil-war economy (1918–21): grain requisitioning, nationalisation and banning private trade.
1921 retreat allowing peasants to sell surplus grain and small private trade, after the Kronstadt revolt.
Bolshevik secret police founded in December 1917 under Felix Dzerzhinsky, central to the Red Terror.

questions.prompt: Which event most convinced Alexander II that reform was necessary?
questions.explanation: Defeat (1853–56) exposed Russia's backward economy, army and serf-based society.
Peasants gained personal freedom but often received poor land and paid redemption payments for 49 years.

questions.statement: Alexander II was assassinated in 1881 by members of the revolutionary group People's Will.
questions.explanation: His death led Alexander III to reverse liberal reforms and rule through reaction.

questions.prompt: Match each figure to their role.

pairs.right: Led the Bloody Sunday petition march

questions.explanation: Tsarist governments mixed modernisation with repression.

questions.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.
Why did Nicholas II survive the 1905 revolution?
options: The October Manifesto split liberals from radicals, and the army stayed loyal
questions.explanation: Concessions divided the opposition, peace with Japan freed troops, and repression crushed the Moscow rising.

questions.text: The 1905 promise of an elected Duma was the October ___.
questions.explanation: The Fundamental Laws of 1906 then reasserted the tsar's autocratic power.

questions.statement: Stolypin's land reforms aimed to create a class of prosperous, loyal peasant landowners.
questions.explanation: His 'wager on the strong' let peasants leave the commune, but progress was slow before 1914.

questions.prompt: Which national minority suffered particularly from pogroms and discriminatory laws under Alexander III?
questions.explanation: The May Laws of 1882 restricted Jewish settlement and occupations; many emigrated.

questions.prompt: What was a major weakness of Witte's industrialisation?
options: It relied on heavy taxes on peasants and foreign loans, and created a discontented urban working class
It was opposed by foreign investors
questions.explanation: Industrial growth was rapid in the 1890s but social tensions in the cities fed the 1905 revolution.

questions.prompt: Why was Nicholas II's decision to take personal command of the army in 1915 a mistake?
options: He was blamed for defeats and left government to the Empress and Rasputin
It ended the war too early
It made him popular with workers
questions.explanation: The tsarina's influence and Rasputin's reputation discredited the dynasty.

questions.text: Lenin's 1917 programme calling for 'all power to the Soviets' was the April ___.
questions.explanation: Its slogans of 'peace, land and bread' won support as the Provisional Government continued the war.

questions.prompt: Put these events of 1917–18 in order.
questions.explanation: March, April, July, August/September, October (November New Style) 1917, January 1918.

questions.statement: The Bolsheviks won a majority in the Constituent Assembly elections of November 1917.
questions.explanation: The Socialist Revolutionaries won the most seats; Lenin closed the Assembly after one day in January 1918.

questions.prompt: How did the Kornilov affair help the Bolsheviks?
options: Kerensky armed the Petrograd workers, including Bolshevik Red Guards, and Bolshevik support surged
It ended the war with Germany
questions.explanation: The Bolsheviks gained majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow soviets in September 1917.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its description.

pairs.right: 1918 peace with Germany giving up large territories

questions.explanation: These measures show how the Bolsheviks survived through force and pragmatism.

questions.prompt: Which was a key reason for Red victory in the civil war (1918–21)?
options: Control of the central industrial heartland and railways, and Trotsky's leadership of the Red Army
Large-scale help from Britain and France
Peasant support for the restoration of the tsar
questions.explanation: The Whites were divided, geographically scattered and associated with landlords and foreign intervention.

questions.text: In March 1921 Lenin introduced the ___ Economic Policy.
questions.explanation: NEP was a tactical retreat after Kronstadt and peasant revolts; the same congress banned factions in the party.

questions.statement: The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was formally established in December 1922.
questions.explanation: Lenin died in January 1924, leaving no clear successor.

questions.prompt: Which historian is associated with seeing the October Revolution as a coup by a small party rather than a popular revolution?
questions.explanation: Pipes stressed Lenin's conspiracy; social historians such as Fitzpatrick and Alexander Rabinowitch highlight real popular radicalisation.
